## My request:
I'm wondering if these differences could be the equivalent to the difference between △ meaning 'trine' or △ meaning 'fire.' It could mean either even within the same page. In some sections things might mean one thing; in another they might mean something different.

items.text: Yes—both ideas are plausible, and they make different predictions: a symbol whose meaning depends on context, versus different ways of expressing the same relationship. I’ll read Claude’s discussion and compare it with what our tests actually checked. 🐍

items.text:
**Yes. Both are live possibilities—and we shouldn’t automatically explain scribal differences away as meaningless variation.** Your Jupiter example gets at a distinction our spelling tests haven’t addressed well enough. 🐍

There are two different mechanisms here:

| Possibility | Your example | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Context changes the meaning** | `△` means “trine” here and “fire” there | The same sign performs different semantic jobs |
| **Expression changes while meaning stays constant** | “Jupiter opposite Neptune” versus “Jupiter and Neptune in opposition” | Order, word forms and connecting words change; the relationship stays the same |

Both could operate within one manuscript—or one page.

**A section-wide vocabulary count cannot distinguish them.** More `-dy` in one section could reflect different terminology, different grammatical constructions, preferred abbreviations, or different ways of expressing the same facts. It doesn’t directly tell us which.

There’s also a useful difference between your triangle examples. In “Jupiter △ Neptune,” the triangle connects two entities. In a list of substances marked `△`, it might assign a property. **Its position and companions help specify its job.** That is something we can investigate without knowing its pronunciation.

Your Jupiter sentences illustrate why our shared-opening test is narrow. A writer might preserve the same subject and relationship while moving them around, adding connecting words, or using a shortened expression. Failing to find shared beginnings weakens one particular written template; it does **not** dispose of relational lists.

I would qualify two conclusions in Claude’s discussion.

**“The effect follows the scribe, not the herbs” is stronger than the reported comparison establishes.** Taking his reported results as given—I’ve read the discussion, not rerun his scripts—the comparisons show that the original herbal effect changes substantially after separating text varieties. They don’t establish what causes the remaining difference. The pharmaceutical A comparison also lacks the herbal A effect, so “it’s simply A” isn’t sufficient either.

Currier variety, scribal hand and transcription are distinct comparison dimensions in existing research too. They shouldn’t become interchangeable explanations. [Lindemann and Bowern’s corpus description](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.14697)

**The `od` decomposition remains a candidate, rather than a recovered core.** One small but consequential correction: our exact contrast is:

`q + ody` ↔ `ar + ody`

That does not automatically establish `qo-` and `ar-` as equivalent qualifiers. Splitting it as `qo + d + y` instead changes the proposed core. We need to compare those alternatives consistently. Claude’s acknowledgment that ordinary two-letter strings might produce similar results is exactly the right unresolved control.

**The better next comparison has two directions:**

- **Within a hand:** does a component change companions or position when the apparent job changes? That could expose context-dependent use.
- **Across hands:** when an independently justified object or relationship stays constant, does one writer consistently express it differently? That could expose the equivalent of your two Jupiter sentences.

So we should sometimes hold the scribe constant—and sometimes deliberately compare scribes while holding the referent constant. Always restricting ourselves to one hand would prevent us from testing your second idea.

For `otar arody`, that means preserving the **whole inscription and its possible relationship to the pictured object**, while allowing alternative internal divisions. We don’t yet have a secure matching referent elsewhere, so we cannot claim a paraphrase or translation.

**Your proposal changes the target from “which strings look alike?” to “which expressions might be doing the same job?”** That is the course correction we need.

items.text:
**Yes—substantial differences, alongside a shared stock of word parts and vocabulary.** The sections look like different uses of a common writing system, although that doesn’t establish what the differences mean. 🐍

I checked the existing transcription across sections. Here, “prefix” means a recurring written beginning—not yet a grammatical prefix with a known meaning.

These are rounded percentages from the H transcription:

| Section | Words starting `qo-` | Starting `ok-` / `ot-` | Ending `-dy` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Herbal / botanical | 10% | 10% | 12% |
| Astronomy / astrology | 2% | 28% | 12% |
| Bathing figures | 24% | 10% | 30% |
| Small plants / pharmaceutical pages | 11% | 13% | 9% |
| Final starred paragraphs | 17% | 15% | 20% |

**The clearest contrast is astronomy versus running text.** Astronomy/astrology strongly favors `ok-`/`ot-` and rarely uses `qo-`. Much of that section consists of short inscriptions and circular writing, so this could reflect **what the text is doing**—naming things versus describing relationships or instructions—as well as its subject.

The similarities are useful too:

- Beginnings such as `ch-` and `sh-` remain common across sections.
- Many complete spellings recur across very different contexts.
- The same ending families recur, but their proportions change.
- In this descriptive comparison, **herbal and pharmaceutical vocabulary are especially close**, as are **bathing-section and starred-paragraph vocabulary**.

That last pairing is interesting for our working-text hypothesis: the final entries may share terminology or writing conventions with the bathing section. It doesn’t yet establish that both contain medical instructions.

**The biggest complication is that differences also occur within one subject section.** Among herbal running text:

| Conventional text variety | Words ending `-dy` |
|---|---:|
| Currier A | About 6% |
| Currier B | About 23–25% |

Both transcriptions preserve that large difference. “A” and “B” are labels for text varieties, not established different languages. This means we cannot simply conclude that an ending identifies a topic: it might instead reflect a writing variety, scribal convention, grammatical construction, or encoding practice.

The large rosettes face needs separate treatment: its available readings are partial and differ from our main transcription coverage. I haven’t folded those figures into the table as though they were directly comparable.

**For finding meaning, I think the strongest question is now:** when the *same candidate content* moves between a short label and a longer passage, which parts stay constant, and which change?

That is exactly why `otar arody` remains useful. We can investigate whether `arody` persists as a possible reference while surrounding components change with the text’s job. That offers a more constrained route than assigning a meaning to `qo-` or `-dy` from section frequency alone.

[Full section profiles, vocabulary examples, and comparison limits](C:/Users/lewis/.codex/visualizations/2026/10/22/01a16529-fd24-7d02-99e0-9a5bef58ed94/section-profiles-v1/FINDINGS.md)
